fact_sheet.business_description: The Company comprises a leading daily newspaper, other publishing properties, and broadcasting stations [D01]. It operates primarily as a provider of news and entertainment, selling audiences to advertisers [D01, D06].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Newspapers: 516,000 daily circulation; advertising space sold to local/national advertisers [D01, D06].
Broadcasting: Entertainment and news programming; audience sold to advertisers [D06].
economics: Capital intensity: $8.820m plant purchases in 1972; $30m newspaper capital-improvement program cited [D02, D06].
Pricing power: Established local positions may limit competition, though advertising is cyclically sensitive [D01, D05].
earnings_record: 1972 earnings growth: Comparable earnings before extraordinary items rose 47.6% [D03].
competitive_position: Newspapers: Post holds nearly 63% of metropolitan advertising linage; Sunday circulation more than twice the remaining competitor [D01, D06].
Broadcasting: High-margin segment (24.42%) but faces regulatory license renewal challenges [D05, D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Debt: $35.436m long-term debt as of FY1972 [D02].
Cash: $29.850m (cash plus commercial notes) as of FY1972 [D02].
Financial needs: Heavy ongoing capital requirements for plant/office projects [D02, D06].
management_and_capital_allocation: Management: Family influence and leadership noted; limited outside control [D01].
Dividends: Doubled quarterly rate to $0.10 ($0.40 annual) in January 1973 [D03].
price_and_valuation: Earnings yield: ~16% pre-tax (based on operating income) [D04].

yields_pct.basis: Trailing earnings yield = 2.02/27; dividend yield = 0.40/27; long bond = 10-year Treasury yield [D04].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Television license renewal challenges in Miami and Jacksonville [D05].
Rising costs at the Post (labor, materials, services) [D05].
Minority shareholder inability to influence policy or force asset sales [D05].
recent_events: July 1972: Daily News closed, reducing newspaper competition [D07].
March 17, 1973: Annual report released disclosing license challenges and proposed Hartford station purchase [D07].
berkshire_context: No existing the Company stake; purchase ledger unavailable [D08].
missing_data: Exact May 1, 1973 market price; maintenance versus growth capital expenditure breakdown; exact current cash position.

understandable.evidence: The business operates a dominant daily newspaper and local broadcasting stations, which are understandable, durable businesses that provide news and entertainment to local audiences [D01, D06].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: The newspaper holds a 63% share of metropolitan advertising linage and has effectively reduced local competition, demonstrating a clear local monopoly position [D01, D06, D07].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Operating income has shown consistent growth from $17.346m in 1968 to $21.806m in 1972, reflecting a strong core franchise [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The company maintains a very strong balance sheet with $29.850m in cash versus $35.436m in long-term debt, resulting in minimal net debt [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The business requires heavy, ongoing capital expenditures for plant and office projects, which dilutes the return on capital [D02, D06].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Management has demonstrated shareholder awareness through dividend increases and successful navigation of competitive landscapes [D03, D07].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: The business is of a size that allows for a meaningful position in the current era of the partnership [D01, D02].

price_screen.evidence: The pre-tax earnings yield of ~16% is significantly higher than the ~1.5x requirement relative to the 6.72% long bond yield [D04].

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a dominant local media franchise with high returns and a strong balance sheet, notwithstanding its capital-intensive newspaper operations

gate2.why_available: The market is currently fixated on temporary regulatory headwinds concerning broadcasting license renewals and general cyclical anxiety regarding advertising spend [D05]. We believe these factors ignore the underlying dominance of the newspaper franchise, which has recently benefited from the elimination of its primary local competitor [D07]. Value will be realized through continued high-margin cash generation and the durability of its monopolistic local advertising position [D01, D06].
evidence: Post holds 63% of metropolitan advertising linage and has seen competition decrease with the closing of the Daily News [D01, D07].
Operating income grew significantly to $21.806m in 1972 [D02].
Pre-tax earnings yield of ~16% provides a significant margin of safety relative to the long bond [D04].
Broadcasting license challenges are standard regulatory hurdles rather than structural impairments to the core business [D05].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market views the company as a cyclical, capital-intensive newspaper operator facing regulatory risk in its broadcasting segment, justifying a modest P/E multiple [D04, D05].
what_must_be_true: The core newspaper franchise retains its pricing power despite cyclical advertising sensitivity.
Broadcasting license renewals in Miami and Jacksonville are successfully navigated.
The management remains disciplined in capital allocation despite family control.

gate3.owner_earnings_per_share: Approximately $2.02 based on 1972 EPS, assuming maintenance capex is reflected in historical operating performance [D02].

key_assumptions: Newspaper franchise maintains dominant 63% ad market share [D01].
Broadcasting licenses in Miami and Jacksonville are renewed [D05].
Operating income sustains growth from 1972 level of $21.806m [D02].

gate3.price_vs_value: Price of ~$27 is roughly 77% of $35 low-end valuation; provides reasonable margin of safety for a dominant franchise.
gate3.alternatives: Long bonds at 6.72% [D04] are inferior to the prospective 16% pre-tax yield on a dominant local newspaper franchise [D04].
gate3.downside_case: Regulatory loss of broadcasting licenses or severe advertising downturn; downside is limited by dominant print franchise and net cash position [D02, D05].
flagged_assumptions: Normalization of owner earnings uses trailing 1972 EPS [D02].
Maintenance capex is assumed to be fully captured in 1972 operating results [D02].

gate4.role_description: permanent_passive_holder — We are buying a stake in a wonderful business at a fair price, and we intend to hold our shares for the long pull, benefiting from the compounding of the business's intrinsic value [D01, D06].
value_realisation_path: Rational capital allocation by management [D03, D07]
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In 1973, we are looking to accumulate high-quality franchises with durable competitive advantages; as we do not seek to control the company, we act as permanent passive holders relying on the strength of the business's local monopoly [D01].

kill_criteria: Broadcasting license renewal is denied by the FCC in Miami or Jacksonville [D05].
Newspaper advertising linage share drops materially below the current 63% monopoly position [D01].
Capital expenditure requirements for the newspaper plant escalate beyond cash flow generation capacity [D06].
Management fails to maintain disciplined capital allocation or dividend policy [D03, D07].
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain enough cash to ensure the insurance operations and any unforeseen contingencies are protected [D02].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Comparison with holding long-term bonds yielding 6.72% or retaining cash for future bargains [D04].
gate5.decider_reason: The investment represents a high-quality, durable media franchise within my circle of competence that I can evaluate as a whole business.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: Regulatory action by the FCC regarding broadcasting licenses could impair the value of our most profitable segment [D05, D06].

valuation.owner_earnings: Approximately $2.02 per share based on 1972 results [D02].
valuation.downside_case: Regulatory impairment of broadcast licenses or sustained advertising downturn mitigated by dominant newspaper franchise and strong balance sheet [D02, D05].

drivers.driver: Price vs value — the company sells for ~$27 per share against an appraised intrinsic value of $35–$45, providing an initial pre-tax earnings yield of ~16% compared to 6.72% for long bonds [D04].

Management has shown shareholder awareness by doubling the quarterly dividend rate to $0.10 in January 1973 [D03].

final.what_would_change_our_mind: Regulatory action by the FCC stripping the company of its broadcasting licenses or a fundamental structural loss of the newspaper's advertising dominance would force us to reconsider the investment [D01, D05].
final.memo:
The Washington Post Company is a classic example of a wonderful business that we can understand and admire. It operates a dominant daily newspaper and a group of broadcasting stations that effectively sell audiences to advertisers [D01, D06]. The newspaper business is a local monopoly, as evidenced by its 63% share of metropolitan advertising linage, a position recently strengthened by the closure of its primary competitor [D01, D07].

Economically, the business is a powerhouse. Operating income has climbed steadily from $17.346 million in 1968 to $21.806 million in 1972, demonstrating the durability of its franchise [D02]. While the newspaper business is capital-intensive and requires ongoing investment in plant and equipment, the broadcasting segment provides high-margin cash flow, with operating margins reaching 24.42% in 1972 [D02, D06].

Management has proven to be able and shareholder-oriented, as shown by their recent decision to double the quarterly dividend rate [D03]. They continue to navigate the competitive landscape effectively while maintaining a balance sheet that carries minimal net debt [D02, D07].

Mr. Market is currently fixated on temporary regulatory headwinds regarding broadcasting license renewals and general cyclical anxiety about advertising spending [D05]. We believe these worries are misplaced and ignore the underlying strength and permanence of the company's local franchises [D01, D06].

At a price of approximately $27 per share, the company offers an initial pre-tax earnings yield of roughly 16%, a figure that compares quite favorably to the 6.72% yield available on long-term bonds [D04]. We estimate the intrinsic value to be between $35 and $45 per share, providing a comfortable margin of safety [D04].

We intend to act as permanent, passive holders of this business. Our primary risk is regulatory, specifically the potential for the FCC to challenge broadcasting licenses in Miami or Jacksonville [D05]. If these licenses are maintained, we expect the compounding of the business's intrinsic value to provide excellent long-term returns [D01, D06].
